title: THE MAN WHO DIED TRYING TO TELL DAVID GOOD NEWS
paragraphs: THE MAN WHO DIED TRYING TO TELL DAVID GOOD NEWS

Everyone thought the battle was over. David had won. His throne was safe. A messenger was running toward him with “good news.” But the king was waiting for the answer to only one question—and when the truth finally reached him, victory sounded like a funeral.
There is something you need to know before we go any further.
The title is supposed to make you stop.
But Scripture makes us correct something immediately.
Ahimaaz did not die trying to tell David the news. The Cushite messenger is not recorded as dying either.
And once you realize who it was, this story becomes far more painful than the title.
Because the dead man was the king’s son.
And somewhere between a battlefield covered with the aftermath of rebellion and a father sitting anxiously between the city gates, a man started running.
He thought he was carrying good news.
That is where this story becomes frighteningly personal.
Because sometimes what looks like victory from the battlefield feels completely different when it reaches the heart.
Second Samuel 18 is not a neat story about heroes and villains.
A kingdom bleeding from wounds that began long before anyone picked up a sword.
And behind all of it stands David—a man who knew both scandal and grace.
David had written songs of worship.
David had been called and anointed by God.
And David had also committed terrible sin.
He committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged the death of Uriah. When Nathan confronted him, David finally stopped hiding:
But forgiveness did not mean that every earthly consequence disappeared.
Grace is not God pretending sin never mattered.
Grace is God refusing to abandon the repentant sinner to the condemnation that sin deserves.
And now David was living inside a house fractured by consequences.
His son Absalom had rebelled against him.
The son wanted the father’s throne.
The father had been forced from Jerusalem.
Yet before the battle, David gave his commanders an astonishing order concerning the very son attempting to overthrow him:
“Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom.”
Listen to the father inside the king.
David knew Absalom was a rebel.
David knew soldiers might die because of Absalom.
David knew his kingdom was being torn apart.
But Absalom was still his son.
Somebody reading this understands that kind of love.
The child who broke your heart is still your child.
The person who betrayed you is still someone whose name can make your chest tighten.
You can know someone is wrong and still grieve what is happening to them.
You can establish boundaries and still cry.
You can hate what sin has done without ceasing to love the person trapped inside its consequences.
That is the emotional landscape of 2 Samuel 18.
And Ahimaaz, son of Zadok, sees something every messenger longs to see:
“Let me now run, and bear the king tidings…”
The Hebrew vocabulary underneath this scene is powerful.
The biblical root is בָּשַׂר — basar, carrying the idea of announcing or bringing news, often good news.
The related noun is בְּשׂוֹרָה — besorah, news or good tidings.
Ahimaaz looks at the battlefield and sees victory.
The king’s enemies have been defeated.
But Joab knows something Ahimaaz has not emotionally processed.
This is not the day for you to carry these tidings.
Then Joab sends a Cushite who had witnessed what happened.
But Ahimaaz cannot let it go.
And Ahimaaz runs so hard that he overtakes the Cushite.
A king waiting between the gates.
Until the watchman sees him in the distance.
David hears about him and assumes:
There is news in his mouth.
Then the watchman recognizes the runner’s movement.
David responds that he is a good man and must be bringing good news.
And the first word out of his mouth is extraordinary:
Shalom carries a rich range of meaning involving peace, welfare, well-being, wholeness and safety.
God has delivered the king from those who rose against him.
Everything he is saying sounds victorious.
And David responds with one question.
“Is there shalom for the young man Absalom?”
He has run faster than the man carrying the complete answer.
He has reached the king with victory...
but he cannot bring himself to say what the king most desperately needs to know.
He says he does not know what happened.
And David tells him to stand aside.
That may be one of the most haunting pictures of modern Christianity.
We can become very good at running.
And still arrive without the answer wounded people desperately need.
You can outrun everyone and still not be ready to carry the message.
You can have speed without courage.
A Bible verse without biblical character.
You can shout “peace” while avoiding the wound sitting directly in front of you.
And David asks him exactly what he asked Ahimaaz:
And suddenly the military victory disappears behind the sound of a father breaking.
David goes up to the chamber above the gate.
And then Scripture gives us one of the most agonizing cries in the Old Testament:
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom!”
Then David says words that should stop every Christian who knows where the biblical story eventually leads:
“Would God I had died for thee…”
I wish I could have died instead of you.
The father wishes he could die in the place of his rebellious son.
But David cannot rewrite what has happened.
He cannot climb backward through history.
He cannot take Absalom’s place after death has already claimed him.
He cannot trade graves with his son.
And where David could only cry, “Would I had died instead of you,” Jesus actually gave His life for sinners.
David is not Jesus, and every detail of Absalom’s story should not be forced into an allegory.
But Scripture unmistakably brings us eventually to the greater Son of David, Jesus Christ, whose substitutionary death accomplishes what human grief could never accomplish.
Christ did not merely stand over humanity’s rebellion and wish He could rescue us.
“The Son of man came…to give his life a ransom for many.”
And the King came looking for rebels.
That is the scandal of grace.
Christ willingly bore judgment for His people.
The cross does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross says your sin was so serious that redemption required the blood of the spotless Lamb of God—and that the love of God was so astonishing that Christ willingly gave Himself to save sinners.
That is why Christianity is not self-improvement dressed in religious language.
Jesus did not die to make you better at hiding.
He died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God.
Repentance means the hiding can end.
Grace means you can finally tell the truth.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Because perhaps you have been Ahimaaz.
People expect good news from your mouth.
you are terrified someone will ask the one question you do not want to answer.
“Are you still secretly going back to that sin?”
“Are you actually following Jesus—or just maintaining the appearance that you are?”
And maybe Jesus is touching the place you have spent years protecting.
To bring you into the light.
Because there are questions we can avoid with people that we cannot avoid before God.
You cannot fool the One who sees the heart.
You cannot curate your soul before an omniscient God.
And that sounds terrifying until you remember who is calling you out of hiding.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who welcomed the broken.
The One who called people to repentance.
The One who went to the cross.
The One who walked out of the grave.
So stop running merely to be seen running.
Stop confusing religious activity with spiritual life.
You do not need to impress Jesus with your speed.
You need Jesus to save you.
If something hidden has been exposed while reading this, do not turn conviction into another five minutes of scrolling.
And if you already belong to Him but have wandered, come home.
Grace is not permission to keep rebelling.
Grace is the open door through which repentant sinners return.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Do not underestimate what sharing biblical truth can do.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list smiling publicly while privately collapsing.
Someone who has not prayed honestly in months.
Someone who thinks they have gone too far.
Someone who needs to discover that the Gospel is not about pretending the scandal never happened.
It is about what Jesus Christ can do with a surrendered life after the scandal.
But hear this clearly because biblical truth matters more than conversion numbers:
Your standing before God cannot be purchased by supporting a ministry.
Buying Christian merchandise cannot make God love you more.
Sharing this article does not earn righteousness.

Yet if this ministry is bearing good spiritual fruit in your life, voluntarily supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping that work continue and helping biblical resources reach more people.
Because Ahimaaz could run quickly, but speed could not heal David.
David could win a kingdom, but victory could not resurrect Absalom.
David could wish to die for his rebellious son, but wishing could not exchange their places.
And He did not merely wish He could die for sinners.
Not that our past was clean.
Not that our families were never broken.
Not that our choices produced no consequences.
Not that our stories contain no scandal.
Our hope is that Jesus Christ still saves sinners who come to Him in repentance and faith.
So when your past whispers your name...
when shame opens an old file...
when the enemy reminds you what you did...
when someone remembers the version of you that you desperately wish you could erase...
Remember that Christianity is built around a Savior who specializes in resurrection.
Some messengers run carrying news of a victory. Jesus came carrying the scars that made our victory possible.
